title: Contextual Models — the BERT Family
summary: BERT-style pretraining — the encoder side of the Transformer story, and when it beats calling an LLM.

slides.subTitle: The same word, a different vector per context
slides.markdown: Contextual embeddings solve the polysemy problem static embeddings couldn't: instead of one fixed vector per word, the model computes a word's vector fresh, **at inference time**, from self-attention over its actual surrounding sentence. "Bank" in "river bank" and "bank" in "bank loan" enter as the same input token but leave BERT's layers as measurably different vectors, because attention pulled in different neighboring context each time. This is the direct payoff of the Transformer architecture applied to representation learning: the same subword-tokenized input, but the meaning is resolved dynamically rather than looked up statically.

slides.subTitle: Masked language modeling and next-sentence prediction
slides.markdown: BERT pretrains on unlabeled text using two self-supervised tasks. **Masked Language Modeling (MLM)**: randomly mask ~15% of tokens and train the model to predict them from the surrounding (bidirectional) context — this is what forces BERT to build genuinely bidirectional representations, since predicting a masked word requires looking both left and right. **Next-Sentence Prediction (NSP)**: given two sentences, predict whether the second genuinely follows the first in the original text, or is a random sentence — intended to teach sentence-pair relationships useful for QA and inference tasks. Later work (RoBERTa) found NSP added little value and dropped it, keeping MLM as the core signal — a good reminder that not every pretraining objective in a paper turns out to matter equally.

slides.subTitle: Classification, NER, and QA heads
slides.markdown: BERT's pretraining produces general-purpose contextual representations, not a task-specific model — fine-tuning adds a small task head on top and updates weights (usually the whole network, at a low learning rate) on labeled data for the target task. **Classification**: a linear layer on the special `[CLS]` token's final representation. **NER**: a linear layer applied to *every* token's representation, predicting an entity tag per token (sequence labeling). **QA**: two linear layers predicting the start and end position of the answer span within the input passage. The key insight: the expensive part (learning language structure) happens once during pretraining; fine-tuning is comparatively cheap and fast, often just a few epochs on a few thousand labeled examples.

slides.subTitle: BERT vs GPT
slides.markdown:
The single biggest architectural difference between BERT and GPT is what each token is allowed to see during training. BERT (encoder-only) lets every token attend to every other token in both directions — natural for understanding a complete input. GPT (decoder-only) masks future tokens, so each position only attends to itself and earlier tokens — necessary for autoregressive generation, where future tokens don't exist yet at inference time. See [Attention & Transformer Architecture](attention-transformer-architecture) for the underlying masking mechanism.

slides.subTitle: Pooled BERT output for semantic search
slides.markdown: For tasks needing a single vector per sentence or document (semantic search, deduplication, clustering), you pool BERT's per-token outputs into one vector — commonly the `[CLS]` token's representation, or a mean over all token vectors. A caveat worth knowing: raw off-the-shelf BERT `[CLS]` embeddings are mediocre for similarity search out of the box; models specifically fine-tuned for sentence embeddings (Sentence-BERT and similar) produce far better similarity rankings, because vanilla BERT was never trained with a similarity objective. This pooled-embedding approach is exactly what powers the retrieval step in retrieval-augmented generation — see [Retrieval-Augmented Generation](llms/retrieval-augmented-generation) — where you embed a query and compare it against pre-embedded document chunks.

slides.subTitle: Understanding tasks vs generation tasks
slides.markdown:
| | Encoder-only (BERT) | Decoder-only (GPT) |
|---|---|---|
| Context per token | Full bidirectional | Causal (left-to-right only) |
| Natural fit | Classification, NER, extractive QA, embeddings | Open-ended generation, chat, few-shot prompting |
| How you use it | Fine-tune a small head on labeled data | Prompt directly, or fine-tune for generation |
| Typical model size | Smaller (110M–340M params common) | Ranges up to hundreds of billions |

How to decide: if the task is *understanding* a fixed input and producing a label or span (classification, extraction), an encoder-only model fine-tuned for the task is often cheaper, faster, and just as accurate as prompting a large decoder-only LLM. If the task is *generating* open-ended text, decoder-only is the only real option.
